utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al., thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record today Mr. Beara's back, but Mr. Popovic isn't. I recall seeing the waiver, your client's waiver, Mr. Zivanovic, for yesterday. I don't recall seeing it for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We will provide the waiver for today as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I don't recall at all having seen any waiver from your client, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning -- or good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. He did execute it, but there was a little problem with it and we will be filing a short motion addressing it and obviously giving you his acquiescence to have proceeded yesterday in his absence. So you will get that in written form tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Representation, Prosecution it's Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer. Defence teams are full force today. I don't see any absences. Witness Momir Nikolic is present, as is his counsel, Mr. Tansey. Yesterday, we left off with your -- you finishing your cross-examination. I just want to make sure, since you were a little bit undecided, hesitant at the time, whether you have any additional questions you would like to put, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, madam. Mr. Josse, I confirm that you have no cross-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. No cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Haynes, he's all yours. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And good afternoon from me, Mr. Nikolic. You're on the last leg now, and I'm going to try and be as quick as I can with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you start, Mr. Haynes, I'm just putting this to you and then you let us know via the registrar: We've just been informed by the Prlic Trial Chamber that they will not be sitting tomorrow morning, and therefore we have the courtroom available should you prefer to sit in the morning. We are all in agreement here. It would be fine with us to sit in the morning, but of course I know that you have a new witness coming in. I don't know whether you need to proof him. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mr. President. I believe he has been fully proofed. We just need to send a quick e-mail just to make sure that he will be available tomorrow morning. We will be -- as far as the team is concerned, we're ready to go, we just need to make sure he's ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And as far as the other Defence teams, if you have any problem with sitting in the morning, please let us know and we'll then sit in the afternoon. Otherwise, we'll sit in the morning thank you. Mr. Haynes, my apologies for the interruption. I should have done it before. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Before you came here, Mr. Nikolic, do you recall that together with your lawyer you prepared a short document explaining what you now accepted and did not accept in your original statement of facts?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during the course of preparing that document, you explained that whilst you have been in prison in Finland you'd had the opportunity to read and digest a book on the principles of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that I had an opportunity to study this book. I only focussed on one section in particular, and I can tell you which section of that book I familiarised myself with. So to make things clear, I never read the whole book. I read only one part, and I tried to comprehend it as much as I was able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very helpful. Was that not a document that was available to you in the preparation of your defence for your trial before 2003?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, because I haven't seen this document. It may have been the case that my lawyers had this rule and the books that you're referring to, but I myself did not have a chance to get myself acquainted with the rule and the book all the way up until before my transfer to Finland to serve my sentence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Again that's very helpful. And when did you set about studying this book and this rule? Was it soon after your sentence or more recently?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you that it was while I was in the detention unit in Scheveningen. That was when I first saw the book and had it in my hands. That was in the detention unit here in The Hague, maybe two or three months prior to my transfer to Finland. In that period, the final judgement has been pronounced already in my case. My trial had been finalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Then I'm sorry for not listening to you more carefully. So in any event, you had read and considered that rule before either of the occasions when you gave evidence in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received translation that I gave testimony. I would like to make it clear that I gave evidence twice before the court in Sarajevo. For the first time I was a court witness, and the following time I appeared as the witness for the prosecution, but I didn't give any statements. If you are referring to my testimony, then this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That is what I'm referring to, and all I'm interested to know is that when you gave evidence there, it was against the background of having read this book and this rule that you referred to in the qualification of your statement of facts.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I already told you when I read the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would be right to understand, wouldn't I, that you do not pretend to be any sort of expert on military law or principles?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, you're right. I'm no expert, but I nonetheless try to grasp and fathom these matters as much as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. And more to the point, you knew how the system worked in 1995, and you knew what your job was.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more specific, please? What system are you referring in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll come to the point. In practice, officers from superior command organs could give orders directly to you, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle I know perfectly well who can issue orders to whom within the chain of command, and you put it well when you said that it's a comprehensive system. If you are interested in any particular feature of the system, I can give you an answer, but I can only tell you that in principle I know who is entitled to give orders to whom and how this whole process is practiced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it might be simpler, therefore, if I remind you of something you've said earlier, and really for the benefit of the interpreters we'll put it in e-court so that they don't get annoyed with me speaking too quickly. It's P4482, starting at page 15 in the English and page 7 in the B/C/S. And so that you understand this, Mr. Nikolic, this is the transcript of what you said when you gave evidence in the case of Milorad Trbic in Sarajevo. Now, the section that I'm interested begins in English with the question at line 14 in English: "Is it fair to say that it's only the brigade commander who could order you to a task? Is that correct, sir?" And you responded: "Yes, in theory. So the commander was my superior as well as the superior of all the others in the brigade command. However, in practice there are certain deviations from this theory. So in principle, yes, that's correct, but in practical life there are some situations when the commander is unable to issue orders, then somebody from the brigade command will issue orders in the commanders's stead. And still, you will go with those rules, with those orders, and you will act upon them." And the question is asked: "Can you explain the circumstances of these deviations?" And you said: "Well, I can. In the situation when the commander is absent from the place, when there are certain combat operations underway, and, for example, corps commander is present but brigade commander isn't, at the time the combat operations are under way in the AOR, area of responsibility, of your brigade. Then, the most superior commander from the highest command can issue orders in your commander's stead. Following the completion of the task or the assignment in any case and in every case the commander is to inform his direct superior whom he was issued order from whom he received orders from, and it is his obligation without exception. This is what he has to do following the execution or action upon orders issued by higher authority." And then you're asked: "Let's just clarify that. You stayed for the occasion when the brigade commander is not present but he is on other duties but within the area of responsibility of the brigade, that, for example, the corps commander can then issue orders for a brigade; is that correct?" And you said: "Not for a brigade, but he can issue orders to me personally." Is that still, in your view, a correct statement of how things worked in practice? And I apologise if you're squinting at the screen. It needs to go one page on in the B/C/S, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question, although I didn't read the whole passage, and I know what you're asking me. If I were to explain this again now, although I really don't want to presume to be an expert in the area of command and control and knowledgeable about the relations in the command structure, I myself was never a commander, and I cannot say with any degree of certainty that something is 100 per cent correct or not. I would like, though, to confirm that what you have read just now is how I understood the question that was put to me, and I did my best to provide an explanation and an answer. I still believe that these questions relating to command and control and the commander is not from the area of responsibility or is and absent from the unit. I would explain it, of course, without repeating the whole statement verbatim, but what I would tell you now would in essence be identical. So if the commander is absent, he designates someone who stands in for him, and then this person issues orders in the name of the commander. I know that this is how it should function, and that is how it functioned. As for the area of responsibility of the brigade, I believe, although I'm not sure, that if the corps commander wants to issue an order to one of the brigade units, then it would be most appropriate and proper in military terms that he should do that through the commander of that unit. However, if the situation is such that the brigade commander is absent from the zone while the corps commander is present, I believe that the corps commander can give orders personally if so required by the current situation; although, as I said, this is not quite appropriate, but if the circumstances are such that they cannot wait for the brigade commander to return, then they resort to this procedure. I'm not sure whether this is fully correct and in compliance with the military law to the full, but in principle I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to tidy this one up, can you explain to us what you meant when you said in your answer in the Trbic case, "the most superior commander from the highest command"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. What I meant here was a special situation that did happen and can happen under such circumstances. Namely, there are combat operations being carried out in a certain area, and it's not within the zone of responsibility of one brigade. Let's take the Bratunac Brigade as an example. If combat operations are being conducted in the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade and the brigade commander is not accessible and reachable in that area and the situation demands that the task at hand must be amended and issued to the unit engaged in the operation, and you don't have the most senior officer in the brigade who is entitled to amend his previously made decision, then, hypothetically speaking, depending on the specific situation, it is only natural, and I think it is in line with the military rules for the decisions in such situations to be made by the most senior officer, both in terms of his position and his rank, who is currently present in the area where the combat operations are being carried out. So it's only logical that if in the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade there is an officer from the brigade and an officer from the corps command and another officer from the Main Staff and the officer from the Main Staff or that from the Drina Corps, according to their position and their ranks, are most senior there, then it's only logical for them to issue specific orders to deal with the specific combat situation. This is how I understand it. And I think I read it somewhere that this is fully in accordance with military rules. However, I always want to -- to emphasise that I have reservations when I'm talking about command and control, because I don't have command and control experience and I'm not an expert in this field. I always have reservations when I am talking about these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Mr. Nikolic. And just to conclude this topic, as you told us the other day, irrespective of the lines of command and control, never in an armed force do you question an order or a request from an officer of your superior command. That's what you told us on the 21st of April. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a blanket confirmation of your thesis or claim. I can only speak for myself. I am almost convinced that I had never refused to carry out an order from a superior command, although at certain points -- or even, sometimes these orders did not personally suit me. But, I did not refuse to carry out orders, because I thought that such things had been agreed at higher levels, so I never presumed to double-check or comment the orders that were coming from superior commands. So generally speaking, I did carry out my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's see if we can apply what you've told us to a practical situation. You told us during the course of your evidence about some military policemen from the Bratunac Brigade who ended up in Pilica. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, but that's not the way I put it. I said that I came to know and see at a later date from a military police log-book that a military police patrol between the 16th and the 17th of July had been kept in Pilica. That's what I said, had been left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And Pilica is not within the brigade area of the Bratunac Brigade, is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Applying what you've told us, if a colonel from the Drina Corps or the Main Staff had issued orders to that patrol of military policemen, it would have been obliged to obey them, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope so -- or, rather, I assume so, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on from there. I'd like you just quickly to look quickly at another document, please. It's our P107, and you better have a look at the front page first so we can identify it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen the document. This is an order for active combat activity issued by the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if I understand the accounts you've given previously, you did not see that order in July of 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified about that and said that I had not seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like us now, please, to go to page 5 in the B/C/S, page 7 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it. I wouldn't want to read the entire page. Tell me the passage I'm supposed to direct my attention to. Probably the one related to the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Correct. And I'm very sorry, that's a reasonable request. The section I want to direct your attention to is just four lines from the top in your language, and it reads: "Security organs and military police will indicate the areas for gathering and securing prisoners of war and war booty." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I heard you correctly, you said the security organs and the police. What I can see here is the security organs will send out instructions to the subordinate units concerning the application of the regimen in the combat activity. So the military police is not mentioned here. I apologise if what I heard was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. If -- are you referring him -- I think you should be referring him to the second paragraph on page 5 in the Serbo-Croat language. Is that correct, Mr. Haynes or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's the fourth line that begins [B/C/S spoken]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the section -- yes, okay. Which, to my knowledge --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we can all work out is the security organ and the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. And this is why I'm intervening because I see Vojna Policije, and I think he may have been reading some other paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you count four lines town from the top, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. I was reading the paragraph below that one. Of course I'll read relevant paragraph. Yes. You're right, sir. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, irrespective of whether you actually saw this document, did you become aware as a security organ that it was your responsibility, in relation to the operation towards Srebrenica, to indicate areas for gathering and securing prisoners of war and war booty?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I understanding was and how I worked both in times of peace and war, and since I took part in countless military exercises in relation to this particular duty of the security organ is as follows: At the stage when the security organ takes decisions and issues orders, et cetera, the security organ plays a role of a proposing party where the organ will propose to the commander where the military police should be deployed, et cetera, and that's the only thing that the security organ, or the intelligence and security organ, does in relation to this type of order. The commander, for his part, can accept or fully reject the proposal, or simply accept it in part. Once the commander has heard all the proposals, including the one about the status of the prisoners of war, the commander will take a decision which will be a definitive decision and binding upon all those who contributed with their proposals and all the various matters concerning the provision of combat security, which includes the matters you refer to. I was aware of that, and that's the way I worked. Whenever I was supposed to I proposed matters to the commander that lay within my competence. However, I have to give you an additional clarification. If you do not take part in the formulation of the written order or in the process of giving proposals, and the commander can decide not to accept proposals. If you don't know what the commander's decision was and if you don't receive the order the commander has written, including -- so if you're not in the -- among the addressees or among those who are supposed to be copied the order to, you will not know what the commander has decided, and it is his discretionary right to decide not to inform you thereof. In such cases, the commander will have taken the decision on his own. And since in accordance with the rules of engagement the commander is entitled to take decisions on his own, independently, he will likewise be taking full responsibility upon himself for the decision taken. That's formulated in the rules of engagement as the commander's discretionary right. That's what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we'll approach it a different way. Did you in fact indicate areas where prisoners from Srebrenica could be gathered and secured?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If your question is whether I proposed the specific areas to my commander, I did not, because my commander did not hold that sort of a working meeting and did not ask my opinion. I testified about this in the previous trials. If you look at my commander's order, you will see that he did not write in the order that I should be delivered the order. He said that the commanders of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th Battalions should be sent the order, the Chief of Staff, the filing service, and that's all, I think. The regular procedure would have been where I would have proposed to the commander the various areas where the prisoners should be gathered and kept. That was the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So in -- in what context was it that you mentioned the Ciglana brickworks and the Sase mine that you told us about the other day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the Sase mine and the Ciglana brickworks in the context of the locations that were discussed as possible locations for the execution of the prisoners in Potocari who were detained in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And the rings and necklaces --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me this -- allow me to add something that I have not testified about so far. At a later date, once the entire operation was over, I learned that certain individuals were indeed touring the area of the brickworks. As for the area of the Sase mines, none the officers toured the area. For the sake of the truth, I also wish to say that these locations were discussed, but not a single killing or execution was ever committed in any of these locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were being asked questions the other day by Mr. Ostojic, you discussed at some length some rings and necklaces and cash that was in your safe. Would those items properly be described as war booty?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I had to say, and you'll be able to look at it from the record, I did say in answer to Mr. Ostojic's questions. There is nothing to take away or add. I can provide additional explanation if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's a simple question. Were those items war booty from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That follows from the hand-over record. You can see that it was war booty, and you can also see it from the minutes of the briefing of the 16th of July where I briefed the commander on this and asked him what was to become of the war booty. In that same document, you have an earlier item, an earlier paragraph, containing the order of -- of the commander where he had already decided about the fate of the pecuniary funds. It is not quite clear from the document that they were referring to funds, to money, but I'm telling you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's forget about what you told your commander allegedly on the 16th of July. How did those items come to be in your safe in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what their provenance was. I think I explained that to one of the lawyers here. And they came to be in my safe because the military police didn't have a safe. Zlatan Celanovic, who was in charge of the entire procedure surrounding this, did not have a safe that would have been intended for keeping such items. For this reason, the items were left in my safe based on a document until such time as the commander issued his order.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Issued his decision," interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In simple terms, rings and necklaces and cash that was taken off people found its way to you through the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to the Bratunac Brigade through the border police which had received the items from the security organs from Serbia. I don't know if it was the police or who, because the individuals on whom these items were found were captured in Serbia. The war booty was seized from them. A record was made thereof. The items were handed over to the board are police, which in turn handed it over to the Bratunac Brigade police. The items I'm referring to include the money, gold, jewellery, everything that was present in my safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who was the first person who told you that any of the former inhabitants of Srebrenica were to be murdered?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my evidence so far, I stated quite clearly when it was that I heard of this for the first time. I've already testified about this. To my questions as to what was to become the fate of those who were captured, I was told that all the balijas had to be killed. I don't know what sort of inference you would make upon hearing something of the sort. What sort of a conclusion would you have arrived at, and what would you have thought had you been in my shoes and had you seen people being separated who were not military-aged men, who had nothing to do with the army whatsoever. And I'm stating this again. People were separated who had nothing to do with the army, with combat, with crime, had nothing whatsoever to do with individuals who could in any way have been held responsible for crimes or war. Had you been in my shoes and seen the treatment they were accorded in Potocari, I put it to you that you would have arrived at the same conclusion that I had upon seeing all that. I had heard quite enough. I did not need to hear somebody utter the words, "They will be killed," but the reaction where it was said that the balijas had to be killed was quite sufficient for me to come to that conclusion based on my common sense. Let me underline again that I would be the happiest man had all this not happened. You can tell me whatever you want. You can try and persuade me that this had not indeed happened. However, my assessments and the conclusions I drew, were confirmed. They were confirmed as true. You will not succeed in discrediting me, because I speak the truth and the truth is on my side. I have the courage to tell the truth, and believe me when I say that I feel lighter, I feel better when I tell the truth and admit that a horrific crime had indeed happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It may have been lost in translation or -- or perhaps you didn't listen to my question carefully enough. All I asked you was who told you that. It only requires a name, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already answered that question ten times in this courtroom. The first time I had my doubts, when I felt that these were things that were portending evil, that was outside Hotel Fontana when I spoke to Popovic, Kosoric, and Petar Uscumlic was there as well on the 12th of July, 1995. That was the first time I realised that evil will take place. That may have been a bit earlier, even, on the evening of the 11th when the second meeting was being held. At that point some requests, demands were put forth where the Muslim units were asked to come to Potocari, to lay down their weapons. They were told that no harm would come their way, that they should surrender. I know that that would have only been logical and soldierly and that that's the way things should have happened. However, I likewise knew having spent four years there previously, I knew the extent of the hatred between the Serbs from Bratunac and the Muslims in Srebrenica. I knew how much blood had been spilt in the meantime and I was almost certain that things could not have ended in a good way, that they had to end in a bad way. I repeat, I didn't need to be said that to my face. Everyone, of course, avoided saying something of the sort, but evil things have happened, sir, and I find it hard to speak about it even now, but I must.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Nikolic, just to clarify the transcript, page 18, line 10, we have the name that you mentioned conspicuously absent in the transcript, and I'm going to read out a small part of the transcript and then you repeat the name, please. "The first time I had my doubts when I felt that these were things that were portending evil. That was outside Hotel Fontana," I suppose, not phone, "and it was when I spoke to," and here we have a name missing. Who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat that for the record. I spoke there with Colonel -- or sorry Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic and Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you named one more individual, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said that on that plateau just before the start of the meeting Petar Uscumlic, the interpreter, was also present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just moving on in the piece, who was the first person that told you that the prisoners held in Bratunac were to be moved to Zvornik for execution?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified about that, too. The first person I heard from that the prisoners would have to go -- would have to be moved to Zvornik was Mr. Beara [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And as I understand the position, not long after that you received an order from Colonel Beara to go to Zvornik and speak to Drago Nikolic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you inform your commander before going to Zvornik that Colonel Beara had given you that order?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Even though the order involved you being out of the brigade area for four or more hours?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I did not inform my commander, Colonel Blagojevic, that I was supposed to go to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on from there. Again, I'm going to read something you have told us the other day when you were being asked questions by Mr. Thayer. It was on the 21st of April, and if anybody wants to check the transcript, it's page 32916. He asked you: "Again, focusing on the intelligence picture that you had going into the morning of the 12th of July, had you received more information about the whereabouts of the Muslim men from Srebrenica that morning?" And your answer was: "Yes. Already in the morning of the 12th and later on even more intensely information started pouring in that elements of the Muslim forces who were pulling out towards Muslim-controlled or free territories were in the Jaglici and Susnjari sectors and that they are using this axis for pulling out of Srebrenica." Now, is that correct that during the 12th of July information as to the whereabouts of the column and its intentions was pouring in?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had information about the approximate area that they were gathering as well as the direction which they were trying to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I apologise if this seems like the same question, but there's a reason why I ask it. By the evening of the 12th of July you had good and reliable information about where they had assembled and the direction in which they were heading, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, sir, information is information. How reliable the piece of information is is something you can't know. If on the 12th you received a piece of information, you first need to follow up on it and check it. What we had was not information, only reports. Let me make it quite clear. The extent to which the information was reliable or accurate was unknown. We received information from the units that were in the immediate area and in contact. You will know yourself that when it comes to information, you have to verify certain things. You have to investigate if they are true or not. What we had was just the first reports about the position of the Muslim column which was present in the area. Similarly, you have to understand that there were around 16.000 people there. That's the information that I had. There were approximately 16.000 people present in the area. You can only imagine what sort of a location can receive 16.000 people. They must have covered a considerable area. These matters are neither precise, nor can one take any decisive or important decisions on their basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But during the 12th of July you were receiving intelligence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nikolic, because we are receiving interpretation in French, and I know Mr. Bourgon doesn't like it. Yes. I hope it's all sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to, as it were, just list the sources of the information. You were receiving intelligence from your own units pouring in on the 12th of July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only confirm that intelligence was arriving from the units that were able to acquire such information. Those were mainly units deployed in that sector, although it seems to me, but don't hold it to me -- don't hold me to it, already on the 12th there was an exchange of information with the Milici Brigade, which was the adjacent brigade. I'm not sure, but I think that even then they conveyed information to us about the movement and information about the assessment of the intentions of the Muslim forces that were there. When I say the Muslim forces and the Muslim column, I say "forces" because there were lots of men, members of the 28th Division, who were armed and who had set up a standard formation for movement and for breakthrough in military terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. You've helped me with my next question, which was that you were also receiving reports from neighbouring units as to the situation and movement of the column, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during the 12th of July, prisoners were being captured from the column who were being interviewed and giving you information.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I didn't have any prisoners on the 12th. If you are referring to the people taken prisoner from the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as you told us the other day, the information was all supporting other information that the column had gathered in Jaglici and Susnjari and was pulling out on a certain axis towards the free territories.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said in my previous testimony is quite sufficient. I have nothing to add to it. Just as I responded to the questions of other counsel, I am responding in the same way to you. That is to say, we had information coming from different sources. There was exchange of information between Bratunac and Milici Brigades, and I think that on the 12th the Bratunac Brigade had no prisoners from the column, if that is what your question was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. On the 12th of July, you were the duty officer at the Bratunac Brigade, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your deputy or assistant duty officer was Jankovic, and you called him to relieve you at 3.00 in the morning when you went to go and sleep in your apartment in Bratunac. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Other than that -- sorry, Mr. Thayer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think we're all agreed, just so there's no confusion on the record, the Jankovic to whom the witness is referring is Sergeant Mirko Jankovic, the komandir of the Military Police Platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's quite right, and I forgot there were two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you both. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Other than that, as duty officer you would have had to be present in the duty operations officers' office throughout the evening, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there in the evening. I may have taken a break and went out to the kitchen, but generally speaking, I spent all the time in the operations room where the operations duty officer performs his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. And any information that was pouring in, you would have passed on to those who needed to know about it, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I testified to that. Generally speaking, I abided by the procedure of writing reports, passing on information to those who might find them interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, thank you. Can we go back one evening to the 11th of July. On the 11th of July you went to the Hotel Fontana twice, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And after the second visit you even took the Muslim representative back to Potocari. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I took him as far as Potocari. I think I took him as far as Zuti Most, but then again I may have taken him to Potocari. Anyway, my task was actually to escort them to the territory under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So let's be clear about this. Your evidence is on the 11th of July, as a Serbian officer you drove through Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not through Potocari. I may have driven up to Potocari. The UN base and where Mandzic was is a little bit away from the centre of Potocari, which is densely populated area and where the civilians and everybody else was already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But in any event, nobody stopped you on the road?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember being stopped by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Maybe we stopped on Zuti Most, but I don't see Zuti Most as a place where somebody should stop me. If we stopped, it was just pro forma to -- to greet the people or to say something about those who went to the meeting in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note: We had not quite understood the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Haynes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the interpreters have doubts as to whether they have understood the witness. Mr. Nikolic, you said -- excuse me, I'm reading out from the transcript. Perhaps you could tell us if this is correct or whether you would like to clarify anything. "Excuse me. Maybe we stopped on Zuti Most, but I don't see Zuti Most as a place where somebody would stop me. If we stopped, it was just pro forma to --" there is something missing here, "to great the people or to say something about those who went to the meeting in Bratunac." Is this what you basically said or did you say something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that's the essence of what I said. Maybe I didn't phrase it properly, therefore I was misunderstood. The check-point at Zuti Most was manned by a man from my brigade, and of course they knew me. I just wanted to say that I was not officially stopped and checked. If we did stop, that was for those reasons, just to tell them that these were men who were with me are coming back from the meeting. That was actually the essence of what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. If that's satisfactory, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: One of the other events of the 11th of July, which you've recalled to us, was that you wrote a report concerning the existence of able-bodied men amongst the people at Potocari. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again I want to be precise. I drafted a report in which I included my assessment, and I'm constantly underlying. What pertained to the number of men, to the intentions, to the composition of refugees in Potocari. These were all assessments. And it is true that in this information containing these assessments which I passed on to the security and intelligence department of the Drina Corps, and I also informed my command about my assessment, the truth is that this assessment contains information that among the civilians in Potocari there were able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thanks very much. I just want to clarify something you told us the other day, the 21st of April. Not for your benefit, for everybody else it's page 32914. You're talking about the 11th of July, and you said: "That evening I informed members of the command who were present in the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. These are staff officers who were part of the corps command, and of course all this information and intelligence was relayed to my commander as well, which is absolutely a regular procedure, and I'm talking about my commander Vidoje Blagojevic." When you said that to us the other day, what information were you referring to and what officers?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have quoted something which was either mistranslated or was a slip of the tongue, or maybe I misspoke. You mentioned staff officers, and then later on, according to the translation that I received, there was talk and mention of corps officers. So something doesn't tally there. I will try to give you a precise answer to your question. Written information containing all the intelligence that I had on the 11th of July in the evening I conveyed to the security and intelligence department of the Drina Corps. The information contained in the written report was forwarded, or I acquainted members of the Bratunac Brigade command; that is to say, the people who were with me all the time. However -- actually, I -- I informed them about all the information that were -- was available to me at the time. I remember office -- officer Micic being there, I also remember another officer by the name of Stevic. I think that Dragan Trisic was also there, but I can't guarantee that these were exactly men who were present at that moment. Anyway, those were men from the Bratunac Brigade command. In addition to that, the information relating to Potocari and everything else learned about -- or actually was found out by the officers from my brigade. They knew everything, and each new piece of information was discussed in the operations room. They were on duty to do their job just like I was as part of the overall operation, and I can say for sure that they knew everything that I, as an intelligence security organ knew, or had as assessment or has had as information that I was absolutely sure were -- was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, thank you. We can -- we can check the tape to see whether it was mistranslated, but we'll move on from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't want to really dwell on the issue, but I think, and my friend may agree with me, I think what we have is two words in English which sound the same. It's been translated in the transcript as corps. I think based on -- on the witness's answer that what he may have said was translated into whatever the word for core, meaning the central brigade command, and then it was translated as corps because we're so used to hearing corps as in Drina Corps, and that explains why there is this reference to the Drina -- or just to the core officers being present. We can try to resolve it now with a question to the witness or pull the tape. I just threw out that suggestion. I think it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Your comments, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We'll look into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I would have thought that sort of comment should not have been made in front of the witness with his headphones on, but we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, he could offer us his comments if he so wishes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I'd prefer to look into the tape first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's advantageous to have had him hear what Mr. Thayer had to say, but anyway, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder whether we could now have in e-court, please, P4472, pages -- or page 29 in the English and 30 -- I'm sorry, page 31 in the English and page 30 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what you need to read to yourself, Mr. Nikolic, begins at line 8. It's the rather long answer you gave there, and I shall read the English into the record. What you said is: "After the meeting, which didn't last that long, the commanding officers came out and they discussed about the new task. What I learned is that the task, it was about the forces which participated in Srebrenica were to be transferred to Zepa. That was one thing that presumably I learned. The following was that they did not manage to reach an agreement about that, and the reason was simply that there were no intelligence. There was no reliable information regarding the location of the column, I'm referring to the Muslim column, about the movement, about the further targets, and that because of that, one of the participants, and this is, this part I learned later, complained and that they did not accept Mladic's idea to move to Zepa." Now, does that remain your recollection of what you learned had been the discussion at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I still stand by what I said before, and what I stated here relates to what I learned after the meeting. I was very precise there when I said that there was no reliable information or intelligence about the location of the column, and I still maintain that. At that time, there was no reliable information about the whereabouts of the column, because it changed its position by the hour, and it was on the move. We also didn't have any reliable information about their intentions. You have to admit that that was a huge number of armed men, and in absence of accurate and reliable information, one could not reach any speedy decisions about anything else. Therefore, I stand by what I already said, and if you want me to elaborate on this further, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, no, on the 12th, as you told us in this trial, intensely information had been pouring in that the Muslim forces who were pulling out towards Muslim-controlled or free territories were in the Jaglici and Susnjari sectors and that they were using this axis for pulling out of Srebrenica. So this meeting that you recalled in this interview, couldn't have happened on the evening of the 12th, could it, because there was tons of information about where the column was and where it was going.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about this meeting, if we are referring to the same meeting, that is, and I would like to confirm today that I'm not sure when this meeting took place, but on the other hand, I'm absolutely sure that it did take place, and in addition to the question mentioned here, other things happened as well that I learned about, of course, but not through being present in the meeting. In my view, it is of lesser importance whether it was on the 11th or the 12th. The important thing is what was discussed at the meeting and the fact that it actually happened. Now, 14 years later -- well, not only 14 years later but even back then, to which I cannot put any time-frame and I believe that to be absolutely normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the passage I just read you came from an interview you had with Mr. McCloskey at the end of May of 2003. You recall, don't you, speaking to Bruce Bursik about a month before that over the course of about three days?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I expressed my opinion about this issue, and I would really like to repeat once again that I stand by what is recorded in this interview, which was audio recorded, which was an official interview shall, and believe me, I didn't embark on any analysis of this document because those were his notes, and probably had we gone through his notes and had some question been put to me, I would have tried to explain things and that would be actually what I would have said. But these were Mr. Bursik's notes. He noted the things as he understood -- stood them, and I standby by what I said in this official interview, and it is regarding both -- recorded both on tape and in -- and on paper. I'm not talking about the notes, but I believe that they would be of better quality and that there would have reflected -- had we gone through them, they would have reflected my comments and my formulation. But as it is, I do not have any objection to the context of the notes as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can agree, can't we, that both in April of 2003, when Mr. Bursik made a note, and in May of 2003, at the end of May when the interview was tape recorded, you told officers from the Prosecution that the meeting that we've just been talking about took place on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already replied to this question. I spoke about my best recollection. I allow for the possibility, and I'm not an obstinate person who someone who thinks that cannot make mistakes. I agree that it's possible. I'm not sure only about the timing of the meeting. However, as for everything else, I confirm that the meeting to place, and I confirm the substance of the meeting. The only thing that I'm not sure about is the time when the meeting took place. And I think that you can understand when one makes such mistake, because in those days there were numerous visits and meetings in the Bratunac Brigade. Officers from the command, from the corps -- corps units were coming, as well as those from the Main Staff, and there was constant going in and out, and there were endless meetings being held, and believe me, under such circumstances it is possible that I made a mistake. But then I don't think it's relevant compared to what actually happened and what was the crux of the matter. What I am saying, I always try to be the reflection of what happened, what I saw with my eyes, or of which I am convinced that had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is that you did in both of those interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like that question answered, then we can take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead and answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I said, at the time of the interview, I said what I could remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honour, for allowing me to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll try and wrap it up in 20 or 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just so that you understand my position, Mr. Nikolic, I think you got it right in May 2003 when you said this meeting took place on the 11th of July and that you've got no reason to have any dilemma about it. Did I understand your last answer before the break to be to the effect that it is only the date about which you have a dilemma?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had my doubts about the date of the meeting that I believe had been held. There were many meetings held in the Bratunac Brigade. I was referring to that one which discussed matters contained in my evidence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But what I mean is you have no doubt, do you, about, as it were, the circumstances of that meeting and how it fits into the chronology of what you were doing around the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What does it mean how it fitted the chronology of what I was doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll show you what you said during the course of that very long interview with Mr. McCloskey at the end of May 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look again, please, at P4472, page 28 and 29 in the English, page 27 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read this once before, so it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to read it again to you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey said: "We left off yesterday with filling in some details about the Hotel Fontan meetings, and if you could just briefly outline for us what you did after the first meeting at the Hotel Fontana ended?" And you said: "Yes, I believe we started with that part. Actually, we finished with that part. After the meeting at the Hotel Fontana, I went to the command of the Bratunac Brigade, and during that time after the meeting I wrote a report for the superior command, a report regarding the activities that took place that day." And Mr. McCloskey asked you: "And did that report include an estimate of the able-bodied men in Potocari or had that report been done before that?" "A. That, yes. "Q. And did you see any commanders or officers at the Bratunac command when you went there that evening? "A. Yes, I saw a group of officers who came to the brigade command, and according to the information I learned later that group of officers was a group of commanders of the compact group which participated in the operation." Mr. McCloskey asked: "Are you sure you saw those commanders there that night of the 11th and not the next night, the night of the 12th? "A. As far as I can remember, it was on the 11th in the evening." Does it remain your recollection that the meeting you have described about going on to Zepa took place the same night you went to the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I explained and stated what I had to say. Naturally, I stand by everything I said. The events and the chronology contained here reflect my recollection of the events. All of this I've stated on several occasions. I stand by what I said in the statement. I expressed my doubts with regard to the dates and their accuracy. I repeat that this is the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So I just want to be clear about this. Is it the best of your recollection that the meeting you have described occurred the same night that you went to the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I said and everything that is contained herein is, I claim again, the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is it your recollection that the meeting you have described occurred the same night that you wrote the report about the able-bodied men at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Please indulge me and answer it again.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by the statement I gave to Mr. McCloskey and I stand by what I said at the time. I do not rule out the possibility that I made a mistake by stating that the meeting was held on the 12th. I have said this, I think, a dozen times now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was it that caused you to develop a dilemma about this date between June and September of 2003 when you gave evidence in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I came to doubt it. It's just that I am not -- it's not that I am stubborn that way. There is a number of documents that I read, roughly grasp what they stated, and made some sort of a chronology of the events. To the best of my recollection, what I believed to be true was that it was on the 11th. Now, why should I be stating something for a fact that I am not sure of? I don't want to state that something is a certainty. If there is 1 per cent of doubt. I can't say with precision that it was on the 11th since there were a number of meetings. I can't be more precise than that. Despite your insistence, I will not state something of the sort, simply because I am not sure of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We'll move on. You have referred sometimes in your evidence to a man called Trisic. Who was he in the Bratunac Brigade, and what was his function?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragoslav Trisic was Assistant Commander for Logistics in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would his responsibilities have included making sure that the brigade had enough fuel?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was within the competence of a logistics organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And forgive me again if this sounds a very similar question. Did he as part of that function have to monitor fuel usage and ensure that fuel was properly accounted for?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I fully understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, did he have to keep check of how much fuel the brigade was using, how much it needed, and to keep records of how fuel was being used?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only give you an answer on the basis of logic. One of the obligations is to monitor the consumption of fuel, to keep track of that, and to report on the matters to his commander. Whether he actually did that is something I don't know. I suppose he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But that wasn't your job, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular provision of fuel, consumption of fuel, distribution of fuel and everything else was within the competence of the logistics organ. Part of that was the traffic service, which took care of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now -- now, please don't be angered by this question because it's similar to a couple I've asked you before, but who was who first told you about the plan to dig up and rebury dead bodies in the autumn of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time official, and I emphasise official, discussions took place were in the Bratunac Brigade on the part of Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. As for what I know of the initiative, what I heard about it, the initiative to carry out the reburial came from the civilian authorities. That's the extent of what I know. Of course, I can't either confirm or prove that that was indeed the case. My information was that it was their initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And your function in all that, amongst other things, was to monitor, preserve, and control the use of fuel, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I explained to one of the counsel everything that I knew in relation to the operation. One of the my tasks since the military police was involved there, too, and my involvement on the basis of the order of the brigade commander as a result of one of the requests that was put to me was that the fuel which was supposed to arrive and to be used for that operation, that the security organ should monitor and account for the use of the fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you why the security organ had to monitor an account for fuel in relation to the reburial of bodies?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I answered that question too. It was put by one of the counsel, but let me state this once more. I can only assume what the reason was, and that was most probably the case, which was that this operation was supposed to be a secret operation. The reburial was supposed to have been carried out in secret. Hence, the fuel which had to be at their disposal, the distribution, and the consumption thereof, all of it had to be taken care of by the security organ. I explained all this to the counsel who put the question. This was neither a secret operation nor did it resemble anything secret. Had the intention been to keep it secret, that could not be carried out because there were too many resources and individuals involved, the military and political leadership, the brigade. Certain companies were involved from the areas of Bratunac and Srebrenica. Under no circumstances could the operation have been secret. One of the reasons why it was decided that the security organs should monitor the consumption of fuel was precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, thank you very much. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Further Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I understand you must be very tired by now, it's more than a week, but please bear with me for a few minutes. I have three questions which transpired during the course of your testimony, so I will start from -- start with minor thing. During the course of your testimony you referred to Resid Sinanovic as having swum across the Drina and having ended up as a patient in Serbia, and I'm not sure, but I don't think the Chamber had heard the -- such a story before, so could you elaborate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Resid Sinanovic used to live in Bratunac before the war. He was the chief of the public security station in Bratunac. When the hostilities broke out, he moved into the territory of Srebrenica, of the Srebrenica municipality. Once the enclave of Srebrenica fell, he was probably part of the column moving in the direction of Kladanj and Tuzla. He was captured in the area of Konjevic Polje. On the occasion of my first visit to Konjevic Polje on the 13th of July, 1995, members of the Bratunac Public Security Station who had a check-point in Konjevic Polje informed me that they held a very important prisoner who, based on the information at the disposal of both the MUP and the army, had been qualified as a war criminal. After my stay in Konjevic Polje, I took over Resid Sinanovic with another policeman, went to the Bratunac, and I handed him over to Jankovic Mirko, the chief of the military police, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the other name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- who was a lawyer, who, in other words, was an interrogator, one who would investigate into -- investigate facts and events. Once he was taken to the police, Dragan Ivanovic and other individuals who used to be close to him before the war within the police. They brought him cigarettes, food, gifts. I don't mean gifts exactly, but whatever foodstuffs he requested. Once Zlatan Celanovic interrogated him and took his statement, and I don't know on the basis of whose decision this happened, because I couldn't decide on these matters, I learned from my conversations with him that subsequently he decided independently that he should transfer him to the school together with the other prisoners because he felt that there were no grounds for keeping him in custody and interrogating him any further. He transferred him to the school, and whatever I'm telling you now is what I heard from Zlatan Celanovic, he moved him to the Vuk Karadzic elementary school, whereupon he was transferred to the area of Zvornik in -- as part of the convoy that departed on the morning of the 14th of July. To my knowledge and to the knowledge of my lawyers who investigated the matter, he was probably taken out, as were all the rest. He was shot at and wounded. I don't know where this took place, where these people were executed. He then, in an area just below Zvornik in Banja Koviljaca, just next to the area of Serbia, there he swam to that area and there he went to a cafe where he met some acquaintances of his who transported him from the area where the cafe was to the Banja Koviljaca hospital. Subsequently, according to what my lawyers learnt and told me, he was transferred to Loznica or not. Don't hold me to that, but there is a report produced by my lawyers to that effect. He was then recognised by a doctor, a lady doctor, who used to work in Bratunac but who, upon the outbreak of hostilities, moved to work in that hospital, and she informed the police in Bratunac that Sinanovic was in the Banja Koviljaca hospital. They then proceeded to inform their services thereof. Now, the subsequent information about when he was taken over from the hospital, the research conducted by my lawyers indicated that he was taken over by the police of the Republika Srpska and that he was liquidated on the bridge at the border crossing between Serbia and Republika Srpska, that's to say Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's the extent of what I know. The documents, the proof that he was given treatment in the hospital was something that my lawyers handed over to Mr. McCloskey during one of the meetings that they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I wonder whether you could give us the time-frame of his death.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't. I think that all the relevant details are contained in the document produced as a result of the investigation carried out by my lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. For my next question can we bring up P4480, page 3 in English, and I take it it's on page 4 in B/C/S. Mr. Nikolic, this is a report or the information sheet the Prosecution produced after having had a conversation with you in 2007 at the place where you are serving your sentence. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 4 in B/C/S, and page 3. You were asked by Mr. Ostojic, representing Mr. Beara, about this passage, I will quote -- probably it's at the top of page 4: "The witness also -- excuse me -- the witness also stated that Beara had nothing to do with the burial of the bodies at Glogova and that Dragan Mirkovic had lied about this because of his friendship with Borovcanin." As to the source of your information, you were asked by Mr. Ostojic whether it was Mr. Mirkovic that told you about this, but you denied, but subsequent intervention made your answer unclear. So my question is what your source of knowledge, that Beara had nothing to do with the burial of the bodies at Glogova, was? How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said what is contained in the text here. Based on everything I learned in the period between the operation and today, I am completely convinced that I must not claim anything with certainty, but I am convinced that Colonel Beara had nothing to do with the burial at Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether you could be a bit more specific as to the source of your information.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that I saw anything. There is information to -- speaking of the activities that happened after the crime, that happened on the 13th at Oka and along that line. There were also activities which took place on the 13th of July in Bratunac in the public security station where a meeting was held chaired by Mr. Dragomir Vasic. The machinery that came from Zvornik was something that Mr. Beara, to my knowledge, had nothing to do with. He had no ability to secure them, nor did he secure the machinery. Based on what I know, it was Mr. Vasic who provided for the machinery that was brought over to Glogova and which was used to bury the bodies. What I found out was that I have my doubts about the participation of a member of the Bratunac Brigade. He took over allegedly the machine, and I do have my doubts about him taking part in the burial on that date, because the information I have, all of it points to the fact that he participated in the burial at a later date, not on that day. Another thing that I deem very important is that Mr. -- or, rather, Colonel Beara had no reason whatsoever to be occupied with the burial of those killed in that area. I don't see that there's a single reason why he would be doing that. This is what I was guided by. I don't know what the actual truth is, and I don't want to speculate. This is what I can tell you based on the information I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. My last question is related to your answer given to Mr. Thayer in the course of answering the question as to the chain of command of various units that were operating in Potocari on 12th and 13th. For the benefit of counsel, it's page 32928, from line 8. I quote: "All forces that were engaged in Srebrenica operation and the operation of forcible transfer from Potocari were commanded and controlled by the Chief of Staff, General Krstic, and the commander of the Drina Corps. Of course, once General Mladic was in the field in the area of Bratunac, then of course it was well known that it was General Mladic who made decisions ordered through his subordinate officers, those being commanders of the corps, brigades, and all other units that took part in Operation Srebrenica." Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What interested me is the term you used, that is, the "operation of forcible transfer," or just simply "forcible transfer." What did you mean by saying "forcible transfer"? If you could explain it to me.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, of course. I have to say that this is my personal view and opinion. I was using the term "forcible transfer" of population because I think that no one insane, and I'm talking primarily --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: No one who is sane.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm talking about the Muslims who were in Potocari and Srebrenica, in that area, would accept voluntarily or with delight or with desire to leave their homes and everything that they had. The situation as it was and the hatred that existed meant that after everything that had had happened there was no way they would be able to live together or next to each other. Therefore, each instance of transfer of that kind, in my view, contains an element of force, and that's my opinion. Of course, I think the same about any ethnic community or groups who are forced to leave their homes and their property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards the -- your original statement of facts, you once told us that the -- the formulation in the statements were those of your counsel, not by your personal formulation. Am I correct in so understanding? Can I be more clear -- clearer? You said it is a formulation done by your lawyer and you accepted it. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the statement of facts, then I can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about the statement of facts, I can tell you that in my view there was very little time for everything to be reviewed and analysed. If I told you the chronology of events and how it came about for the statement to be signed eventually, then you would see for yourself that at the time I didn't have an opportunity to fully analyse everything that was written there. Well, after all, I didn't have time to understand everything that was written there. For that reason that's what I said, but of course I unreservedly believed my lawyers at that time, and I presumed that since they were lawyers, they were well-familiar with those affairs. There are some phrases contained in the statement of facts that I do not agree with, because as such they do not reflect what I had been doing, and in that context is why I said that they participated in drafting the statement. Of course, I accepted their suggestions, and I hope that you know that I was supposed to enter a plea on the 6th of May, but that I had an opportunity and a very short time to discuss all these documents and the statement of facts on the very same day, and if I would be given an opportunity to do all -- everything all over again, I wouldn't give them such an opportunity to make decisions on my behalf. But we are where we are. I made a mistake. And I would just like to say that when it comes to the usage of certain phrases, I didn't attach any importance to them, because I thought that it was clear that I, who was not accused on the basis of command responsibility, I cannot be punished for something like that. That is how I understood things at the time. Unfortunately, I wasn't right. And I would have done otherwise now if I had had an opportunity. In other words, I would insist on everything that I said to be precisely and accurately recorded in -- in the words and phrases that I used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I understood fully, but different from the original statement of facts, the -- your further statement or supplementary statement you produced before this Chamber is your own words. You wrote them in person yourself.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the supplemental statement, that is where I made an attempt to clarify everything contained in the original statement and to make it more precise. I also wanted to explain and describe what really took place and the events in which I was involved, but I wanted this to be the reflection of what I was actually involved in. Your Honours, there is one more thing.
